subject: English
summaryPoints: Quantifiers correspond to noun countability: 'much', 'little', and 'a little' modify uncountable nouns, whereas 'many', 'few', and 'a few' modify plural countable nouns; 'some', 'any', and 'a lot of' modify both.
'Little' and 'few' convey a negative meaning denoting scarcity or insufficiency (almost none), whereas 'a little' and 'a few' convey a positive meaning indicating a small but sufficient quantity.

Adverb clauses of reason explain causality using conjunctions ('because', 'as', 'since' followed by clauses), whereas prepositional phrases of reason ('because of', 'owing to', 'due to', 'on account of') govern nouns, pronouns, or noun phrases.
Adverb clauses of manner describe how an activity is carried out using 'as', or depict hypothetical manner using 'as if' and 'as though' followed by past or subjunctive verb forms.

Present perfect tense expresses actions completed in the immediate past (with 'just' or 'already'), past experiences with indefinite timing (with 'ever' or 'never'), and ongoing situations continuing into the present (with 'since' and 'for').

Backformation is a morphological reduction process that derives a shorter base word—typically a verb—by stripping an apparent suffix from an existing noun (e.g., editor -> edit, television -> televise, babysitter -> babysit).

formulas.label: Quantifier Countability Distribution
formulas.expr: Countable Plural: many / few / a few / a number of  |  Uncountable: much / little / a little / an amount of

formulas.label: Semantic Contrast: (A) Few vs (A) Little
formulas.expr: few / little = negative (scarcity, nearly none)  |  a few / a little = positive (some, small but sufficient)

formulas.label: Conjunction vs Preposition of Reason
formulas.expr: Clause of Reason: Subject + Verb + because / as / since + Subject + Verb  |  Prepositional: Subject + Verb + because of / due to + Noun Phrase

formulas.label: Hypothetical Manner Clause
formulas.expr: Subject + Verb(present) + as if / as though + Subject + Simple Past / were

examTip: In EUEE questions, distinguish between 'few' and 'a few': 'He has few friends' means he is lonely and has almost no friends (negative); 'He has a few friends' means he has some friends (positive). Also make sure not to use a complete clause directly after 'because of' or 'due to' without a noun phrase or gerund.

keyDefinitions.definition: A determiner or adjective specifying the quantity, amount, or proportion of the noun being modified.
A subordinate adverbial clause introduced by subordinating conjunctions (because, since, as) explaining why an event occurs.
A subordinate adverbial clause introduced by 'as', 'as if', or 'as though' that demonstrates how an action is performed or mimics reality.
A word-formation process in which a new, shorter word (usually a verb) is created by deleting an actual or supposed affix from a longer existing word.

eueeFocusTopics: Distinction between 'few' vs 'a few' and 'little' vs 'a little'
Clauses of reason ('because') versus prepositional phrases of reason ('because of')
Hypothetical clauses of manner using 'as if' and 'as though'
Present perfect aspect usages (immediate past, experience, unfinished time)
